b: If, as Walter Benjamin has argued, literary afterlife is less a matter of preservation than “a transformation and a renewal,” the posthumous publication of Toni Morrison’s Language as Liberation raises an additional question—how might a writer’s own criticism shift the terms of her legacy?

To examine the uncertain fate of a great novelist’s critical work is to perform a profane surgery on literary prestige, one that exposes the raced, gendered, and classed fault lines along which we sort artistic genius from interpretive authority, intuition from expertise, art from analysis. For a writer as celebrated as Morrison, the danger is that we read her critical achievement only backward—as a record of influence on her novels or a key to deciphering their difficulty.

But Language as Liberation, a collection of Morrison’s lectures for a Princeton seminar titled “Studies in American Africanism,” invites us instead to follow her critical attention outward, into a troubled national canon she neither redeems nor wholly condemns, but reads against itself. The elliptical, at times editorially mediated quality of her readings of familiar figures like William Faulkner, Willa Cather, and Gertrude Stein becomes part of the volume’s ambition. They preserve something less easily apprehended in Morrison’s other published criticism, exchanging polished conclusions for the dynamism of an intellectual practice. Interpretation, we are reminded, is a thoroughly shared undertaking.

In speaking with Claudia Brodsky, a professor of comparative literature at Princeton whose editorial notes and introduction to the collection extend a decades-long friendship and collaboration with Morrison, I was struck by how little our conversation resembled the sentimental reminiscence I had reflexively expected. She described a kind of intimacy borne less from proximity than from a moment of close reading, a habit of overlapping sentences. But even as we understand the relationship behind this book as a profound critical companionship, it ultimately required of her an uncanny reversal. In Morrison’s absence, Brodsky found that their long conversation could continue only if she learned to read the friend she knew so well “like a stranger.”

Lillian Quijano Johnson (LJ): Language as Liberation feels at once deeply inflected by your editorial vision and animated by Morrison’s pedagogical voice. Could you walk us through how the book came together and how your relationship with Toni Morrison shaped the assembly of these lectures?

Claudia Brodsky (CB): I’ll begin with the story of when Toni and I first met. I arrived at Princeton a couple years before she did. She gave a public lecture, which was meant to be a preview before she took up her duties. I was definitely going to this lecture. Although I had just arrived at Princeton, the head of the Humanities Council invited me to the dinner afterward. I was kind of amazed. “What am I, this very young person, doing here?” There were five of us total, including Toni and four senior faculty members who were all strangers to her. She was just trying to eat her oysters and negotiate the staid atmosphere in what used to be a very ancien régime French restaurant in Princeton. And then this simple thing happened. I told her, “I heard that metaphor you used.” She turned her whole body to me and asked, “What metaphor?” I can’t remember it exactly, but it was about her relationship to the world of reviewers. After I repeated it to her, she simply said, “Oh, you got that one.” Something shifted for her. The dinner continued as usual, but when we all stood up to go, she said, “Honey, would you mind walking with me to my car?” That walk to her car was only about 20 yards, but it lasted two hours. We were cackling. We just stood there in the street laughing. We talked about everyday things, institutional things, but mostly lots and lots of jokes. I’ve always thought that a lot of comedy is just figurative language. That’s why it works, right? Sure enough, before she got in her car, she asked if I wanted to have lunch the following Wednesday. Then it just continued. We saw a lot of each other wherever we were living. And it was all based on the fact that I heard what she meant.
LQJ: And around what year was this?
CB: Oh, God. I arrived in the fall of ’85, so that was Spring ’87.
LQJ: Such a long collaboration inevitably raises questions about what can and cannot be carried into the form of the text.

CB: Toni always wanted me to write about her work. It was mostly out of frustration with the critical world. She would say, “Oh, Claudia, they’re only doing X, or they’re only saying Y.” With this book, I had originally been asked by Toni’s son, Ford Morrison, to write explanatory analytic essays that would accompany each lecture, which I then drafted over the past two to three years. They did not simply introduce the lectures but offered a reading filtered through Toni’s analyses and contextualized in broader critical conversations about the authors. Toni often lectured on the lesser-read works by canonical American authors, so they needed more framing to translate to a public audience. For instance, she took up Ernest Hemingway’s largely forgotten novel, To Have and Have Not. The novel plays out a boomerang effect. The narrator, Harry, displays such obvious verbal racism even though he has almost no interiority otherwise. Most people don’t know the novel because they’ve seen the famous film version starring Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall. Guess who rewrote it for the screen and made Harry a resistance fighter in Martinique? William Faulkner.

CB: That’s what I said! No way! Because I read the novel for Language as Liberation and thought, How the heck did this get made into a heroic movie? It was so racist, even Faulkner couldn’t bear it. But that was the novel Toni chose to lecture on. Boy, writing the introduction to that work was difficult. It was also very instructive. Only Toni would have found and focused on this work. I was later informed that all of the analytic essays that I worked on, except for the general intro, were going to be excised. Toni was writing the lectures for an undergraduate class, so they were confined to a 50-minute format. My introductions were meant to synthesize and expand on them. Ford Morrison and I still hope to publish those eleven essays as a companion volume to Language as Liberation, so that readers can encounter the fuller analyses of Toni’s lectures and the novels they take up.

LQJ: As I understand it, Language as Liberation is only one node in your ongoing dialogue with Toni Morrison. You also co-edited Birth of a Nation’hood in 1997 and worked together on the 1992 collection of essays, Race-ing Justice, En-gendering Power. As your relationship with her developed, how did you experience the movement between Morrison a public thinker, and Morrison as interlocutor in more intimate intellectual exchanges.

CB: The metaphor anecdote is perfectly exemplary of how things worked for her. Toni didn’t necessarily expect the professional, critical public to understand what she was saying. At times, she expected them to misunderstand almost, if not entirely, on purpose. That’s the nature of public life. It’s filled with a lot of clamor. She was always happy to have somebody who didn’t make more noise—someone who really listened. And as far as she was concerned, if they listened well in public, they would probably make great readers. After I met Toni, she actually shared the first drafts of every novel that she wrote with me.

At the same time, Toni thrived in bringing her thoughts out into the world. She was serious about public discourse. After we worked on Race-ing Justice, En-gendering Power, Toni asked me to introduce and moderate a public discussion on her work at the 92nd Street Y. Before we went onstage, she asked me to field audience submissions ahead of time and read aloud only the “right questions.” She was so sick and tired of being asked, “Do you write with a typewriter, a pen, or a computer? Do you write in the morning, or do you write at night?” Her least favorite question, which she heard repeatedly after she published Paradise, was: “Who is the white woman?” The novel famously opens with the line “They shoot the white girl first,” while otherwise never specifying anyone’s race. It’s a brilliant ruse on her part, and one that many critics took at face value. I wouldn’t allow that question to be asked of her. She really believed that those with whom she shared a more private intellectual and personal life were also the ones who understood what she was doing in her public work.

LQJ: It seems like the candor, humor, and mutual interpretation on which your relationship with Morrison was founded generated a kind of trust that could also accommodate disagreement. Although you each had distinct intellectual commitments, you also shared important points of reference—your work on William Faulkner and Herman Melville, for instance, as well as a concern with Enlightenment epistemological inheritances in literary form. Were there moments when those shared interests led to divergences or productive tension?

CB: Toni and I had the same fundamental feeling about language as a capacity. It was the crux of everything for us. Because we shared that, I’m not sure we profoundly disagreed on anything. She and I often discussed the ways that language was constantly involved in the social construction of reality. For her, this insight was both deeply rooted in her lived experience and reinforced by the literature she was reading.

In terms of critical theory, she was sometimes drawn to a Foucauldian model of power as unilateral and total. I’ve tended to be more skeptical of Foucault, particularly when he underplays the complexity of language. Had we pursued that line of discussion more directly, I think we might have found ourselves in agreement. But we never quite got there. There are many theory-focused interviews I conducted with Toni at her request that have never been published. She wanted a space to think aloud in a way that wasn’t really possible in front of an audience. In those conversations, I tried to bring the content of her fiction into conversation with the modern critical theorists I knew well and admired. She was interested in how others had articulated, in more abstract terms, the same concerns she was working through. We spent a great deal of time on figures like Benjamin, Derrida, and Arendt. Foucault was the one I never mentioned, because I knew it might lead us into a different kind of debate.

I’m more interested in the Frankfurt School. As Adorno famously argued in “Cultural Criticism and Society”—they’re just bookends of each other. The only culture that is worth being culture has to be critical. To my mind, that’s precisely what Toni was doing. In one public talk, she described reading a news story about a gardener who had killed her own child. She called it completely inexcusable. She was a very proud mother. It was inconceivable to her. And thus she had to conceive it. That’s a very powerful Frankfurt School understanding of what culture is supposed to do.

LQJ: Speaking of language, your and Morrison’s accounts of language together suggest that it does not always neatly transmit meaning but is also a site of contestation. Language is informed as much by interpretation and even misreading, as it is by understanding. How should we think about the title of the book, Language as Liberation, in that context?

CB: The power of language is quite unique, right? It acts upon the mind constantly, and it is the way in which most of us relate to one another. It takes a completely obscene, dehumanizing kind of isolation—which even this country hasn’t quite perfected yet—to prevent any communication between human beings from taking place. In that sense, language is liberating. It doesn’t tear down the walls, it doesn’t fight wars, but it definitely makes people do stupid things, and makes other people do smarter things. It doesn’t have a physical force, but it certainly makes physical force take place. Toni and I both felt that very strongly.

In the books that Toni is addressing in Language as Liberation, the language in itself is not liberating—with the exception of William Faulkner. During our first lunch together, we agreed he was our favorite writer in English. She had done her master’s thesis, and I did my undergraduate senior thesis, on Faulkner. In the lectures, she insists that even if one spent their whole life reading Faulkner, they’d never get to the end of it. We agreed about that. He is completely aware of what can be done with language. But in the vast majority of the books on the syllabus, that’s not the case. The course was about a language of race, and that’s often not a liberatory language. Your reading has to be liberatory. Toni really pushed students to see that you had to apply critical reading to some of these books to actually see what they were doing. Ultimately, Toni’s philosophy in organizing this class was that language was certainly not physically liberatory, but that unlocking what’s inside language leads to a mental liberation that can become physical.

LQJ: Building on what you’re describing as this concretized intersection between language, reading, and power, I’d like to ask a bit more about the issue of the canon. In your introduction, you write that our violent and fraught history appears, “not only in the context but in the external evaluations of American literature.” The lectures themselves make clear that the construction, establishment, and maintenance of the literary canon have always been political acts, rather than merely aesthetic ones. In today’s context, do you see the canon as the central site on which literature is politicized? How might that have changed since these lectures were first delivered?

CB: Not by coincidence, it’s only now that James Baldwin is fully recognized as part of the canon and routinely cited. The same is true of Ralph Ellison. When Toni wrote The Bluest Eye, it was famously turned down. She used to recount out loud to me the inventory of publishing houses that refused to publish it and the number of times it’s been censored and taken out of libraries. It’s still taken out of libraries today. But she just kept writing. And it may seem obvious, even outlandish, but The Bluest Eye was the book that reshaped what the American canon could include. And having done so, Toni commenced to make the canon her business. She asked us all to look more closely at it. Not because she hated it—she didn’t! When she wrote the play Desdemona, she wasn’t revising Shakespeare. She merely decided to give voice to Desdemona and her Black servant. The play was what Shakespeare, in other words, suggested to her.

I was much tougher on some of the authors in her lectures than Toni was. Author to author, she was much more forgiving than I. She was not interested in censorship. She wanted her students to understand what was going on in people’s fictional imaginations. What shows up on paper is not just what society expects of a writer, it’s the predisposition of their mind. And that, people needed to see. In this sense, Toni loved teaching. I think she loved literature so much that she understood teaching it as her obligation.
LQJ: I love your description of Morrison’s pedagogical career as a kind of responsibility to literature.
CB: Oh, yeah, she really felt it. It wasn’t busy work for her. It was, number one, make people read. And then make them read attentively. She wanted people to read, not just dismiss.

LQJ: I’m also glad you brought up Ralph Ellison and James Baldwin in your response. I was thinking of them when I read the lectures—along with William Faulkner and Henry James—as both novelists and critics of the literary sphere. Indeed, Language as Liberation leaves us with a strong impression of not only Morrison’s teaching practice but also her critical impulses. I’m curious how you would situate her in a broader history of American literary criticism. How does she align with or depart from other traditions of the novelist as critic?

CB: The best critics in general are not those who hold themselves up as the avatars or protectors of culture, but those who can read the contradictions in any cultural artifact. Toni and I would go to jazz concerts by Keith Jarret, whom she adored for the same reason that I adored him—the tension in his playing. We admired the pure beauty that emerged from his work, but also the different directions it would go in spontaneously. This gives you a sense of Toni’s critical disposition. She liked criticism that was responsive to beauty, but that also did the reading required to describe how beauty took place. She had a very philological bent. It was only the words that counted, and if beauty somehow emerged from them, she wanted to know how.

I once said to her son before we put this book together, “It’s funny, people keep reading Nabokov’s lectures on literature, somehow he was allowed to be a critic.” I’m not a fan of them myself. By contrast Toni was often personified as someone who wrote in a vaguely feminized trance. And yet, she was a professional reader, as an editor and a teacher. And she was a deeply discerning critic. She worked at a level of abstraction that she is rarely given credit for, in part because she was a woman, because of her race, and because she was a novelist. She deserves to be taken seriously as a critic, and she wanted to be recognized as one during her lifetime. To this day, there are people at Princeton who owe their ability to take their own reading seriously to Toni.

LQJ: I want to ask you a bit more about the institutional context of these lectures. The title of the seminar, “Studies in American Africanism,” feels itself like an intervention across several fields at Princeton. What department were they originally taught in?
LQJ: That’s striking. I understand African American studies didn’t officially become a department at Princeton until 2015.
CB: That’s very late in the day, right? Though I think it existed as a program earlier.
LQJ: Yes, it began as a program in ’69.
CB: And barely had anyone to teach it. That was the first year Princeton even admitted women.

LQJ: Exactly, so my instinct is that there is something more complicated historically and institutionally behind the story of African American Studies at Princeton. As you know, the department is now housed in Morrison Hall, which was renamed in Toni Morrison’s honor. I’m curious how she may have understood her role in Princeton’s evolving history with African American studies.

CB: To speak to how that moment at Princeton came together—with such a remarkable concentration of Black intellectuals in the ’80s—there was one person largely responsible for it. The extraordinary Ruth Simmons served as vice provost at Princeton University for many years. She understood that Princeton had a reputation and a history to reckon with. It’s known as the Southernmost Ivy. Southerners would send their sons here with their own slaves in the 19th century. A lot of the streets that surround campus are still named after slave owners. Ruth wanted to straighten this out.

She made a series of key hires. She managed to get Arnold Rampersad, Cornel West, and Toni Morrison at Princeton around the same time. Institutionally, Ruth had a way of persuading Princeton that it could gather these superstars in one place. Why not bring them together, offer a strong salary, and let their proximity to one another generate something larger? Nobody likes to be very much alone in what they do. It was really an amazing thing, and it cut across departments.

Toni invited me to a few of their dinners. I remember everyone looking at me as if to ask, “What is she doing here?” and Toni would just say, “Hi, everybody—meet Claudia.” I felt lucky to be there. And Ruth really made this community possible. She built it and she kept it alive.

Toni was deeply loyal to Ruth, and she valued being within reach of New York. But over the years, a lot of these scholars went to different places. Centrifugal force is a powerful thing. Perhaps when Ruth left, something of that cohesion went with her. It really took one person. She had the will and she found the way.

LQJ: I’ll close with a more personal question. After years of collaboration and co-editing, Language as Liberation must have been a very different kind of project to undertake—one shaped as much by Toni Morrison’s absence as by her presence. Can you speak about what it meant to bring this work together without being able to consult with her?

CB: I once gave a talk at a conference at Princeton on Toni’s work. The talk made her cry. She laughed at herself for doing it. I wasn’t talking about her as if she were absent or no longer with us. She was sitting a few rows in front of me! But she told me that it felt as if she was hearing someone talk about her from some other time.

In some ways, this project felt like a truer dialogue. Over the years, no matter what we were reading or where it came from, Toni and I would find ourselves reaching for the same words. It was uncanny. For this work to come together, in a way, she had to be absent. I couldn’t sit down and ask her what she meant when she said something in a lecture. I had to come at the material like a stranger. I don’t think it could have happened otherwise.
